# SK1050 — Use pattern matching instead of a test-and-cast

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A conversion followed by a null check, a safe cast used only as a type test, or a negated type check is a pattern.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | 7.0 |
| Since | 1.3 |
| ReSharper | `UsePatternMatching` (`resharper_use_pattern_matching_highlighting`) |
| Supersedes | IDE0078, IDE0083 |

## Why

`var b = x as Binary; if (b != null)` converts, stores, and then asks whether the conversion worked — three steps for one question the language has had an answer to since C# 7. `x is Binary b` is one `isinst`, one variable, and a relationship the reader does not have to reconstruct from two adjacent statements. The same holds for `(x as T) != null`, which allocates a conversion result nobody wants in order to test a type, and for `!(x is T)`, which reads as the negation of a question rather than as the question the code is actually asking.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
var binary = node as Binary;
if (binary != null) {
    Visit(binary.Left);
}
```

Write:

```csharp
if (node is Binary binary) {
    Visit(binary.Left);
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **`SK1015` owns `is T` followed by a cast; this rule is the rest of the family and never restates it.** Four shapes: an `as` conversion whose very next statement is an `if` testing it for null, a safe cast compared against null (`(x as T) != null` → `x is T`), a negated type test (`!(x is T)` → `x is not T`), and a type check that succeeds for every non-null value of the operand's own static type (`s is object` → `s is not null`). ⚠ The `as`-plus-null-check shape requires **every** reference to the local to be inside the `if` it guards: a pattern variable is not definitely assigned after the `if`, so a use below it would be CS0165, and an `else` branch is refused for the same reason. The conversion operand must be a chain of plain names, so nothing that could be evaluated for a side effect moves into a condition. ⚠ The tested type must be a reference type — `x is int?` is CS8116 — and a null comparison whose operand type declares `operator ==` is left alone, because `==` there is not the reference test the pattern makes. ⚠ The two shapes that produce a `not` pattern are silent below C# 9 even though the rule's floor is C# 7, and every shape is silent inside an expression tree, where a pattern is CS8122, and where rewriting would change what the tree contains. ⚠ **Not covered, and deliberately so:** `UseSwitchCasePatternVariable` (a `switch` case that casts in its body), `ConvertTypeCheckPatternToNullCheck`, and the negated `as` guard (`if (t == null) return;`), which needs a reachability proof the other shapes do not.
